subject: math
title: Measuring Angles: Benchmark Angles, Protractors and Angles on a Straight Line
seo_title: Grade 5 Measuring Angles Worksheets: Protractor and Benchmark Angles (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Explain how protractors work, use a protractor to measure and construct angles up to 180°, and use benchmark angles to estimate the size of other angles
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 math worksheets on measuring angles for the Ontario curriculum: estimate with benchmark angles (45°, 90°, 180°), compare angles, read the inner and outer protractor scales, name acute, right, obtuse and straight angles, and find angles on a straight line. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Estimate first, then read the protractor scale that starts at 0 on your arm.
key_sub: Benchmarks: 45° is half a right angle, 90° is a right angle and 180° is a straight angle. Acute is less than 90°, obtuse is between 90° and 180°. Angles that make a straight line add up to 180°.
body_html:
Benchmark angles

An angle is the amount of turn between two arms. We measure it in degrees (°). Three benchmark angles help you estimate: 45° (half a right angle), 90° (a right angle, a square corner) and 180° (a straight angle).

Estimate

An angle opens a bit wider than a square corner, but not halfway to a straight line. Estimate it.

It is more than 90° and less than 135° (halfway between 90° and 180°).

Answer: about 110°

The length of the arms does not change the size of an angle. Only the turn matters.

Angle names

NameSize
Acute angleless than 90°
Right angleexactly 90°
Obtuse anglemore than 90°, less than 180°
Straight angleexactly 180°

How a protractor works

A protractor is half a circle split into 180 small turns of 1°. It has two scales, so you can start at 0 on either side. The inner scale starts at 0 on the right. The outer scale starts at 0 on the left.

1. Estimate first: acute or obtuse? 2. Put the centre of the protractor on the vertex. 3. Line up one arm with 0. 4. Read the scale that starts at 0 on that arm. 5. Check the reading against your estimate.

Construct an angle of 70°

Draw a base line and mark the vertex. How do you draw 70°?

Put the centre on the vertex and the base line on 0. Use the scale that starts at 0 on your line, make a dot at 70, then join the dot to the vertex.

Answer: a dot at 70 on the scale that starts at 0

Angles that make a straight line

Angles that make a straight line add up to 180°. To find a missing angle, subtract from 180°.

Find the missing angle

Two angles make a straight line. One is 55°. Find the other.

180° − 55° = 125°. Check: 125° + 55° = 180°.

Answer: 125°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading the wrong scale (140° for a 40° angle)Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm, then check your estimate
Thinking longer arms make a bigger angleCompare how far the arms open, not how long they are
Calling 90° obtuseExactly 90° is a right angle. Obtuse is more than 90°
Subtracting from 360° on a straight lineAngles that make a straight line add up to 180°

faq.q: What do Grade 5 students learn about angles in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: They use benchmark angles like 45°, 90° and 180° to estimate and compare angles, and they learn how a protractor works so they can measure and construct angles up to 180°.

faq.q: How do you use a protractor to measure an angle?
faq.a: Put the centre of the protractor on the vertex, line up one arm with 0, then read the scale that starts at 0 on that arm. Check the reading against your estimate: acute angles are less than 90°.

faq.q: Why does a protractor have two scales?
faq.a: So you can measure from an arm on either side: the inner scale starts at 0 on the right and the outer scale starts at 0 on the left. Reading the wrong scale is the most common mistake.
Benchmark angles are angles you know well, such as 45° (half a right angle), 90° (a right angle) and 180° (a straight angle). Comparing with them gives a quick estimate before you measure.

sets.title: Acute, right, obtuse and straight angles

items.q: What is the name of the marked angle?
items.e: A right angle is exactly 90°, a square corner. The small square shows it. The angle is turned, but turning it does not change its size or its name.

items.q: Which list goes from the smallest angle to the largest?
items.e: Acute is less than 90°, right is 90°, obtuse is between 90° and 180°, and straight is 180°.

items.q: An angle measures 91°. What is its name?
items.e: 91° is more than 90°, so it is obtuse (only just). A right angle is exactly 90°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 100°. The angle is turned, but turning it does not change its size or its name.

items.q: Which angle is obtuse?
items.e: Obtuse means bigger than a right angle. D opens wider than the square corner in B. A and C are acute.
A straight angle is exactly 180°. The two arms make a straight line.

items.q: Which list has only obtuse angles?
items.e: Obtuse angles are more than 90° and less than 180°. 95°, 130° and 175° all fit. 45° is acute, 90° is right and 180° is straight.

items.q: How many right angles make one straight angle?
items.e: 90° + 90° = 180°. Two right angles side by side make a straight line.

items.q: What is the name of the marked angle?
items.e: A right angle is exactly 90°, a square corner. The small square shows it. The angle is turned, but turning it does not change its size or its name.

items.q: What is the name of the marked angle?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 70°. The angle is turned, but turning it does not change its size or its name.

items.q: An angle measures 175°. What is its name?
items.e: 175° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse. It is close to a straight angle, but not 180°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 125°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 145°. The angle is turned, but turning it does not change its size or its name.

items.q: What is the name of the marked angle?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 20°.

items.q: Zoe says an angle of 90° is obtuse because it is a big angle. Is she right?
c: No, it is a right angle
items.e: An angle of exactly 90° is a right angle. Obtuse angles are more than 90°.
A straight angle is exactly 180°. The two arms make a straight line. The angle is turned, but turning it does not change its size or its name.

items.q: An angle measures 89°. What is its name?
items.e: 89° is less than 90°, so it is acute (only just). A right angle is exactly 90°.

items.q: What is the name of the marked angle?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 35°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 160°.
A straight angle is 180°: the two arms make one straight line. A is obtuse, nearly straight, but it still has a bend.

items.q: Which angle is closer to a right angle: 80° or 105°?
items.e: 80° is 10° away from 90°, because 90° − 80° = 10°. 105° is 15° away, because 105° − 90° = 15°. So 80° is closer.
The angle is a bit more than a right angle (90°), but less than 135°. About 120° fits. (60° would be acute.)

items.q: Use benchmark angles. Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is less than half a right angle (45°). About 30° fits. (150° is what the outer scale of a protractor would say.)

items.q: Which list goes from the smallest angle to the largest?
items.e: Compare the hundreds first, then the tens: 59° < 95° < 105° < 150°.

items.q: An angle is a little smaller than a right angle. Which could it be?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. A little smaller than 90° is about 80°. 100° is a little bigger.

items.q: Use benchmark angles. Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle looks like a square corner, so it is about 90°. (It is 88°.)

items.q: Leah’s angle is about halfway between a right angle and a straight angle. What is a good estimate?
items.e: Halfway between 90° and 180° is 135°, because 90° + 45° = 135°. (270° comes from adding 90° + 180°.)
120° is a bit more than a right angle, but less than 135°. C fits. A is acute, B is nearly straight and D is only just more than a right angle.

items.q: How many degrees is half of a right angle?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. Half of 90° is 90° ÷ 2 = 45°. (50° comes from thinking a right angle is 100°.)
The size of an angle is the amount of turn between the arms, not the length of the arms. A opens the widest (about 150°), even though its arms are the shortest.

items.q: Use benchmark angles. Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is about half of a right angle, so it is about 45°.

items.q: Angle P has long arms. Angle Q has short arms but opens wider. Jayden says angle P is bigger because its arms are longer. Is he right?
c: Yes, long arms make big angles
items.e: The size of an angle is how far the arms turn apart. The length of the arms does not matter. Q opens wider, so Q is bigger.

items.q: Which angle is the smallest?
items.e: Look at how far the arms open, not how long they are. C opens the least (about 25°), even though its arms are the longest.
The angle is more than 135° but less than a straight angle (180°). About 150° fits. (30° is the acute angle on the other side.)

items.q: An angle is a little smaller than a straight angle. Which could it be?
items.e: A straight angle is 180°. A little smaller is about 170°. 190° is bigger than 180°.
The angle is about halfway between a right angle (90°) and a straight angle (180°), so it is about 135°.

items.q: Use benchmark angles. Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is more than half a right angle (45°) but less than a right angle (90°). About 60° fits.
The arms almost make a straight line (180°), so the angle is about 170°. (10° is the small gap left to make a straight line.)

items.q: Which angle is closest to 45°?
items.e: 45° is half a right angle. B is about half of a square corner. A is nearly a right angle, C is very small and D is obtuse.

items.q: An angle is bigger than 45° but smaller than a right angle. Which could it be?
items.e: It must be between 45° and 90°. Only 60° fits. 30° is smaller than 45°, and 100° and 140° are bigger than 90°.

sets.title: Read a protractor: inner and outer scales

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 30. (The inner scale says 150 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 30° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 155. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 150 and 160 is 155. The outer scale says 25 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 155° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 100. (The inner scale says 80 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 100° makes sense.

items.q: Why does a protractor have two scales?
c: So you can add the two numbers
One is for big angles only
So you can start at 0 on either side
items.e: The inner scale starts at 0 on the right, and the outer scale starts at 0 on the left. Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm.

items.q: Priya measures an angle that is clearly smaller than a right angle. The arm crosses the protractor at 35 and 145. What is the angle?
items.e: An angle smaller than a right angle is acute, less than 90°, so it is 35°. 145 is on the other scale.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 40. The outer scale says 140 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 40° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 55. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 50 and 60 is 55. (The inner scale says 125 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 55° makes sense.

items.q: One arm of an angle is on 0 of the outer scale. Which scale should you read?
c: the scale with the bigger number
the scale with the smaller number
items.e: Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm. Here that is the outer scale.

items.q: Emma wanted to construct an angle of 50°. Her base arm is on 0 of the inner scale. The picture shows what she drew. What angle did she actually draw?
items.e: Read the inner scale, because the base arm is on its 0: the second arm is at 130, so the angle is 130°. Emma used 50 on the outer scale by mistake. 180° − 50° = 130°.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 65. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 60 and 70 is 65. The outer scale says 115 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 65° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 70. (The inner scale says 110 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 70° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 110. The outer scale says 70 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 110° makes sense.

items.q: Aiden measures an angle and writes 40°. The angle is clearly obtuse. What should he have written?
items.e: An obtuse angle is more than 90°. Aiden read the wrong scale: the other scale gives 180° − 40° = 140°.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 135. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 130 and 140 is 135. The outer scale says 45 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 135° makes sense.

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 20 and the other is at 95. The angle is the difference: 95° − 20° = 75°. (95° comes from reading only one arm.)

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 120. (The inner scale says 60 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 120° makes sense.

items.q: Benjamin wants to construct an angle of 65°. He puts his base line on 0 of the inner scale. Where should he make a dot?
items.e: Use the scale that starts at 0 on your base line: the inner scale. Count up to 65 (the small mark between 60 and 70), make a dot, then join it to the vertex. The small marks go up in 5s, so 5 marks after 60 would be 85. Using 65 on the outer scale would give 115°.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 145. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 140 and 150 is 145. (The inner scale says 35 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 145° makes sense.

items.q: Where do you put the centre of the protractor when you measure an angle?
c: in the middle of an arm
at the end of an arm
items.e: The centre goes on the vertex, where the two arms meet. Then line up one arm with 0.

items.q: Ethan wanted to construct an angle of 70°. His base arm is on 0 of the outer scale. The picture shows what he drew. What angle did he actually draw?
items.e: The base arm is on 0 of the outer scale, so read the outer scale: the second arm is at 110, so the angle is 110°. Ethan used 70 on the inner scale by mistake. 180° − 70° = 110°.

sets.title: Angles that make a straight line

items.e: 180° − 35° = 145°. (55° is 90° − 35°: the line is not a right angle.)
Angles that make a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 110° = 70°. (20° comes from 110° − 90°.)

items.q: Which pair of angles makes a straight line?
The angles make a straight line. What is the missing angle?
items.e: First add the angles you know: 40° + 55° = 95°. Then 180° − 95° = 85°.

items.q: Angles that make a straight line add up to …
items.e: A straight angle is 180°. Two right angles make a straight line: 90° + 90° = 180°.

items.q: A straight line is split into a right angle and two equal angles. How big is each equal angle?
items.e: 180° − 90° = 90° is left for the two equal angles. 90° ÷ 2 = 45°.

items.q: Three angles make a straight line. Two of them are 30° and 70°. What is the third angle?
items.e: 30° + 70° = 100°. 180° − 100° = 80°. (100° is the sum of the two angles, not the missing one.)

items.q: The angles make a straight line. What is the missing angle?
items.e: The small square shows a right angle, 90°. 180° − 90° = 90°, so the other angle is a right angle too.

items.q: Two equal angles make a straight line. How big is each one?
items.e: 180° ÷ 2 = 90°. Each one is a right angle.

items.q: Two angles make a straight line. One angle is 135°. What is the other angle?
items.e: 180° − 135° = 45°. Check: 135° + 45° = 180°. (55° comes from taking 0 − 5 the wrong way round, and 225° from 360° − 135°.)

items.q: The three angles marked a are equal and make a straight line. What is a?
items.e: The three equal angles add up to 180°. 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. (120° comes from 360° ÷ 3.)

items.q: Two angles make a straight line. One angle is twice as big as the other. How big is the smaller angle?
items.e: The smaller angle is 1 part and the bigger angle is 2 parts: 3 parts make 180°. 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. The bigger angle is 120°. (90° comes from sharing 180° into 2 equal parts.)

items.q: The angles make a straight line. What is the missing angle?
Two angles are 100° and 70°. Amira says they make a straight line. Is she right?
items.e: 100° + 70° = 170°. A straight line needs 180°, so they do not make a straight line.
Angles that make a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 55° = 125°.

items.q: The angles make a straight line. What is the missing angle?
items.e: The small square is a right angle: 90°. 90° + 62° = 152°, and 180° − 152° = 28°.

items.q: Two angles make a straight line. One of them is obtuse. What kind of angle is the other one?
items.e: The two angles add up to 180°. The obtuse one is more than 90°, so less than 90° is left: the other one is acute. (For example, 120° + 60° = 180°.)

items.q: Two angles make a straight line. One angle is 72°. What is the other angle?
items.e: 180° − 72° = 108°. Check: 108° + 72° = 180°. (112° comes from taking 0 − 2 the wrong way round, and 18° from 90° − 72°.)
The line is tilted, but it is still straight: 180° − 140° = 40°. (50° is 90° − 40°: the line is not a right angle.)

items.q: Two angles make a straight line. One is 50°. Noah says the other is 310° because 360° − 50° = 310°. Is he right?
items.e: A straight line is 180°, not 360°. 180° − 50° = 130°.

sets.title: Angles in real life: clocks, ramps and more

items.q: What kind of angle do the hands make at 4 o’clock?
items.e: At 4 o’clock the hands are 4 spaces apart: 4 × 30° = 120°. That is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse.
The ground is a straight line, so the two angles add up to 180°. 180° − 20° = 160°. (70° comes from 90° − 20°.)

items.q: A wheelchair ramp makes an angle of 5° with the ground. A skateboard ramp makes 30°. Which is steeper?
items.e: The bigger the angle with the ground, the steeper the ramp. 30° is bigger than 5°, so the skateboard ramp is steeper.

items.q: Maya’s scissors are open 40°. She opens them twice as wide. What is the angle now?
items.e: Twice as wide means 2 × 40° = 80°. (20° is half as wide, and 60° only adds 20°.)

items.q: What is the size of the marked angle between the hands at 2 o’clock?
items.e: Each space between two numbers is 30°. At 2 o’clock the hands are 2 spaces apart: 2 × 30° = 60°. (10° counts 2 × 5 minutes.)

items.q: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 15 minutes?
items.e: In 15 minutes the minute hand goes from 12 to 3, a quarter of the way around: a right angle, 90°.

items.q: In coding class, Sofia’s robot faces north and turns 90° clockwise. Then it turns 90° clockwise again. How many degrees has it turned in all?
items.e: 90° + 90° = 180°. The robot made a half turn and now faces south.

items.q: How many degrees does the minute hand turn from 7:15 a.m. to 7:45 a.m.?
items.e: In 30 minutes the minute hand goes from 3 to 9, halfway around. The start and end make a straight line: 180°.

items.q: What is the size of the marked angle between the hands at 3 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 spaces between the numbers go around the clock, and each space is 30°. At 3 o’clock the hands are 3 spaces apart: 3 × 30° = 90°, a right angle. (15° counts 3 × 5 minutes.)

items.q: A classroom door is opened so that it makes an angle of 100° with the wall. What kind of angle is this?
items.e: 100° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse.
The ground is a straight line: 180° − 35° = 145°. (55° comes from 90° − 35°.)

items.q: Owen measures the slope of a ski hill with a protractor and writes 155°, but the slope is clearly acute. What is the angle?
items.e: An acute angle is less than 90°. Owen read the wrong scale: 180° − 155° = 25°.

items.q: What is the size of the marked angle between the hands at 5 o’clock?
items.e: Each space between two numbers is 30°. At 5 o’clock the hands are 5 spaces apart: 5 × 30° = 150°. (25° counts 5 × 5 minutes.)

items.q: Kai opens a book and lays it flat on the desk. The two covers make one straight line. What kind of angle is that?
items.e: The covers make a straight line, so the angle is a straight angle: 180°.

items.q: At the skatepark, a ramp makes an angle of 25° with the ground. What kind of angle is that?
items.e: 25° is less than 90°, so it is acute. Ramps are usually acute angles.

items.q: Ava opens a laptop so the screen makes 110° with the keyboard. Then she opens it until it is flat (a straight line). How many more degrees did the screen turn?
items.e: Flat is 180°. 180° − 110° = 70° more. (250° comes from using 360° instead of 180°.)

items.q: Chloe’s canoe paddle and the water make an angle of about 45°. Which benchmark is that?
items.e: 45° is half of 90°, so it is half a right angle.

items.q: At which time do the hands of a clock make a right angle?
items.e: At 3:00 the minute hand points to 12 and the hour hand points to 3: a quarter turn, 90°. At 6:00 they make a straight line, and at 12:00 they are on top of each other.

items.q: What is the size of the marked angle between the hands at 6 o’clock?
items.e: At 6 o’clock the hands point in opposite directions. They make a straight line: 180°. (6 × 30° = 180°.)

items.q: A hockey stick’s blade lies flat on the ice. The shaft and the blade make an angle of 135°. What angle does the shaft make with the ice on the other side?
items.e: The blade lies flat on the ice, so the two angles make a straight line: 180° − 135° = 45°.
